text: Dr. Diaa introduces the Al-Tayyibat System, which he describes as a preventive and recovery-oriented approach based mainly on avoiding certain familiar foods and allowing others.
He says the first prohibited category is white-flour products, including many common breads and pastries such as croissants and similar baked goods.
He continues by excluding pizza, pasta, and other flour-based foods, then says all soft drinks and energy drinks are prohibited regardless of whether they are regular or diet.

He says the sugar content is not the issue for him and extends the restriction to other carbonated drinks. He also excludes milk, white cheese, cottage cheese, labneh, yogurt, powdered milk products, and creamers.
He also excludes eggs and chicken. He then begins listing foods he allows, starting with whole-grain bread made from the complete grain and bran.
He distinguishes this from ordinary baladi bread and says rice, freekeh, bulgur, corn, sweet corn, popcorn, and corn on the cob are allowed.
He says cream, butter, ghee, and olive oil are allowed. He also distinguishes processed/yellow cheeses from fresh white cheeses and says many yellow cheeses are permitted.
He says yellow cheeses that melt easily are acceptable, and he also permits sweets such as jam, honey, chocolate, Nutella, and similar products.
He says many sugary foods and packaged juices are allowed. He then says he ranks fruits into categories, with some allowed more freely than others.
He places dates, grapes, figs, bananas, and plums among his preferred fruits, with strawberries and seedless guava below them, and says mangoes and peaches should be limited.
He says kiwi and some melons are excluded in his system. The host then asks for an example of what someone following the system would eat in a normal day.
For breakfast, he suggests whole-grain toast and says it can be bought from supermarkets; he expresses a preference for packaged whole-grain bread over some bakery versions.
He says some bakery bread may contain more white flour for taste. He suggests toast with one of the allowed cheeses and other foods such as potatoes, ketchup, or mayonnaise.
The host asks about fava beans. Dr. Diaa says beans and legumes are excluded and claims fava beans are responsible for many colon problems.
They discuss favism and G6PD deficiency. Dr. Diaa says he will explain why he considers fava beans problematic and says his view is unlikely to change.
He cites a Quranic passage mentioning certain foods and interprets the phrase 'that which is lower for that which is better' as supporting his ranking of foods.
The host challenges that interpretation, while Dr. Diaa maintains that the verse supports his view that some foods are of lower quality.
He says that after developing his theory, he began finding religious references that he felt supported it, and he then looked into traditional accounts of what the Prophet ate.
The host cautions against overextending Quranic interpretation, while Dr. Diaa says the discussion is relevant to his reasoning.
He returns to the food list and says fava beans, cowpeas, beans, peas, and other legumes are prohibited in his system.
He says he ranks vegetables according to fiber, peel, and chlorophyll content, placing potatoes at the top of his vegetable list.
He says potatoes are allowed, then ranks other vegetables such as zucchini and okra below them, while placing green beans and other legumes much lower.
He says legumes are outside his preferred foods and claims they produce irritating waste products and toxins in the body.
He links this discussion to G6PD deficiency, correctly noting that certain people with G6PD deficiency can develop red-blood-cell breakdown after exposure to fava beans.
He also mentions sulfa drugs and aspirin in the context of G6PD deficiency and says people with the deficiency should avoid known triggers.
He then extends his argument beyond G6PD deficiency and claims legumes still place stress on the body and colon even in people without the deficiency.

He says, in his view, fava beans are not suitable human food and claims that people who eat them commonly experience colon or sleep problems. The host then asks how quickly symptoms should improve on his plan.

Dr. Diaa gives very specific timelines for improvement in symptoms such as reflux, irritable-bowel symptoms, pain, insomnia, and fatty liver. These are his claims, not established treatment guarantees.
The discussion moves to meat and fish. He ranks lamb very highly and says he prefers meats with softer, shorter fibers that he believes are easier to digest.
He places goat and similar meats high on the list, then mentions liver from certain animals while excluding chicken liver.
He discusses fish, allowing some types while excluding shrimp and squid in his system, and expresses preferences among common fish species.
He says sea fish is generally preferable to river or farmed fish because, in his view, what an animal eats affects the quality of its meat.
He summarizes his ranking as lamb, liver, camel meat and fish, followed by veal and certain birds.
He says meat texture matters to him: he prefers cuts with fine, tender fibers rather than tougher meat.
He places older beef lower because he considers it harder to digest and says he generally favors foods that are easy to chew and digest.
He says ease of chewing and digestion is central to his approach, then explains why he excludes grape leaves and many leafy vegetables.
He claims leafy vegetables such as grape leaves, arugula, cabbage, and lettuce are very harmful to the colon. This is his view and is not established medical guidance.
He says that outside his list, he believes many people experience symptoms from foods such as milk or chicken, and the host then asks again about his views on meat and protein.
He says protein is not the main component of the meal in his system and argues that bread, cheese, potatoes, rice, and soup can form meals without meat.
He invokes the story of Joseph and grain storage to support his view that grains are foundational foods.
He argues that grains are central to nutrition and says they have been wrongly displaced by an emphasis on vegetables and meat.
He identifies three main grains in his approach: whole-grain wheat, rice, and corn, while excluding pasta because it is a manufactured product.
The host returns to water and flour. Dr. Diaa criticizes diet plans that treat a portion of rice and a portion of pasta as equivalent merely because both are called carbohydrates.
He argues that natural rice and manufactured pasta should not be treated as identical simply through calorie or carbohydrate calculations.
He says providing more raw material, such as amino acids, does not by itself force the body to build muscle, because body regulation is more complex.
When asked how people should know what is beneficial or harmful, he says he does not rely only on specialists and argues that people can observe how their own digestive system responds.
He suggests using symptoms after eating as feedback: if a food repeatedly causes gas, cramps, or digestive upset, he says that food should be avoided.
He says his system is mainly based on abstaining from certain foods rather than adding medicines, presenting it as a relatively simple experiment.
He claims white-flour bread is responsible for many illnesses and asks why people remain sick even when they believe they are eating a nutritionally complete diet.
He argues that many illnesses that were once relatively uncommon have become widespread and uses this as support for questioning modern dietary patterns.
He then discusses chronic illness and asks why some people remain ill for decades, before the host returns to the subject of water.
Dr. Diaa says people should drink according to thirst rather than forcing fixed daily amounts such as two or four liters.
He connects thirst and fasting with his interpretation of cellular renewal, claiming that hunger and thirst help remove older cells.
He describes a cell life cycle in which cells either divide, repair themselves, or die, and he loosely connects failed regulation with aging and cancer.

He names autophagy as part of this discussion and says the body continually renews itself, though some of the signs he gives for liver health are personal claims rather than validated diagnostic methods.

He cites religious traditions about breaking a fast with dates and small sips of water, then claims that drinking large amounts of water can cause health problems. These claims should not be treated as established medical advice.
The host says she personally finds Dr. Diaa's ideas important and says the program will continue the discussion and observe public and professional reactions.
The host criticizes doctors who simply block or dismiss him instead of debating his ideas, and the segment closes with a promise to revisit the controversy.
